The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint regarding disclosure of data by the communications officer of a political party to unauthorized persons, because the data subject had not provided sufficient evidence that their rights were violated.

The Estonian DPA upheld a complaint filed by noyb and declared that the controller transferred personal data to the U.S. in lack of any legal basis under the GDPR. The controller was ordered to stop the processing.

The French DPA fined GROUPE CANAL+ €600,000 after receiving 31 complaints for the failure to comply with several GDPR Articles. The fine relates in particular to ‘cold’ calls, the exercise of rights by the data subjects, safety issues concerning the company's employees’ passwords and the company’s failure to notify the DPA when a serious personal data breach took place in 2020.

The Italian DPA fined a controller €70,000 for unsolicited telemarketing calls, including to individuals registered to the Italian Public Opt-out Registry. The DPA found a systematic lack of GDPR compliance including Articles 5, 6, 12, and 13 GDPR.

A healthcare worker complained that colleagues had repeatedly accessed her health dossier at the Lodi hospital trust in 2019-2020, during the Covid pandemic, to find out her swab results, organise shifts and assess quality of care. The Garante found that the access was for purposes other than treatment, by staff not involved in her care, without valid consent, and that the dossier had no alert or full logging systems. It declared the processing unlawful, fined the trust EUR 40,000 and ordered it to put in place anomaly alerts and full access logging within 90 days. The decision is also published in full.

The Italian DPA issued a warning to a private person for installing a camera on the external wall of her house, which was also covering a nearby playground. The processing operation was in breach of the lawfulness and data minimisation principles.

The Spanish DPA (AEPD) issued a decision on the processing of personal data by CaixaBank S.A., the controller, holding that the design of a cookie banner respected its “Guidelines on the use of cookies” of 2020.

DEYA X violated GDPR's data minimization principle Article 5(1)(c) by sharing an employee's personal and health data with multiple recipients without proper justification. The HDPA ordered DEYA X to create internal policies to ensure GDPR compliance. A fine of 1,000 euros was also imposed.
The DPA held that the media reporting on a leaked file containing PCR test results of several thousand individuals, and the non-disclosure of the source are protected by the journalistic privilege.

The Croatian data protection authority fined the debt collector EOS Matrix d.o.o. EUR 5.47 million after an anonymous complaint with a USB stick holding 181,641 individuals' data. The inspection found inadequate technical security, which meant the company could not explain how the data left its system. It also found processing of non-debtors' data without a legal basis and recording of health details, including diagnoses, without a legal basis or a valid Article 9 exception. Privacy policies wrongly said health data would not be processed, and the wording about call recording ("may be recorded") was unclear. Calls were recorded between May 2018 and January 2019 without a legal basis.

In the context of an Article 60 GDPR procedure, the Cypriot DPA reprimanded a controller for unlawfully asking a data subject’s ID when addressing an access request and for failing to inform its users properly about a data breach.

The Belgian DPA reprimanded a Flemish municipality for violating Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, Article 5(2) GDPR, Article 12 GDPR, Article 13 GDPR, Article 14 GDPR, Article 24(1) GDPR, and Article 25 GDPR, as a result of their insufficient technical and organisational measures, and insufficient privacy policy.

In the context of a procedure under Article 60 GDPR, the Irish DPC reprimanded AirBnb Ireland for infringing the data processing principles of data minimisation and storage limitation and for invalidly relying on Article 6(1)(f) GDPR as a ground for processing, when retaining a data subject's ID documents.

The Danish DPA reprimanded a processor, an all-in-one platform for the real estate industry, for breaching Article 32(1) GDPR. The processor had implemented poor security on its platform since users could view confidential data in the source code simply by accessing the browser developer tools.

A patient complained that, after a pulmonology sleep study, the physician emailed him the report and copied a third-party company supplying ventilation equipment, without his consent. The physician argued urgency of treatment, that the clinic held the patient's consent and that he acted as the clinic's processor. The Garante found he acted on his own, so was an autonomous controller, and had no valid legal basis for disclosing health data to a third party. It declared the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a), (c), (f) and 9 GDPR and fined him EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered since the conduct had ceased. A note says the opposition proceedings ended with a favourable judgment for the physician (Tribunale di Prato, 2025).

The Garante received a report that medical records (prescriptions, patient files, X-rays) were lying abandoned and accessible to anyone in the disused former Banti Sanatorium owned by the Tuscany Centre health authority. The authority argued the site was guarded, the papers were old and mostly illegible, and no retention rules applied. The Garante rejected these arguments, noting that sector retention and disposal rules existed and that patient identifying data were visible in the footage. It found breaches of Article 5(1)(a), (e), (f) and Article 32 GDPR and Article 75 of the Code, imposed a fine of EUR 50,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective measures were ordered because the documents had been removed and disposed of.

The Ministry of Environment published on its institutional website an inspection-related annex containing names and employee numbers of workers at the Taranto steelworks (ex Ilva), including around 45 linked to health data (prescription safety glasses). The documents stayed online for 16 days and were downloaded four times. The Garante found the publication lacked a legal basis and breached the data minimisation, lawfulness and health-data rules. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000, ordered publication of the decision, and adopted no further corrective measures since the data had been removed.

The Finnish DPA ordered a healthcare provider to facilitate the exercise of the right of access and inform data subjects of the possibility of obtaining a copy of their personal data, such as copies of their MRI scans, free of charge pursuant to Article 15 GDPR.

Following a report of a potential data security breach, ANSPDCP investigated the energy company RESTART ENERGY ONE S.A. It found that a file on the website containing personal data of at least 750 people was publicly accessible via search engine links for about two and a half years. It also found non-essential cookies were installed before consent and that refusing them had no effect. The company was fined RON 124,150 (about EUR 25,000) under the GDPR and RON 40,000 under Law 506/2004, and ordered to implement a procedure for regular testing and evaluation of its systems, especially the website.
The Croatian DPA imposed an administrative fine in the amount of €15,000 on a controller due to multiple GDPR violations in the context of its online booking system.
The Spanish DPA fined €600 for installing security cameras that focused beyond the private property of the controller's, violating Article 5(1)(c) and 13 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA fined €17,000 a local Handball Federation for requesting and processing health data of its participants in its competitions to discriminate on the basis of such data, violating Article 9 and Article 13 GDPR.

The Greek DPA carried out an on-site inspection of OASA's automatic fare collection system (the electronic ticket) in November 2019, to check compliance with its earlier opinions 1/2017 and 4/2017. The audit found that the data protection impact assessment was late and inadequate, that no retention period had been set (20 years was later chosen for all purposes without justification), and that the record of processing was incomplete. The Authority fined OASA EUR 50,000 for breach of the storage limitation principle and reprimanded it for breaching Articles 25(1) and 35(1). It also ordered OASA to define and document retention periods within one month and to revise the impact assessment within three months.

The Romanian DPA investigated controller BODY LINE SRL and found that it had violated Articles 5, 6, 9, 17, 32(1) and 32(2) GDPR, because an employee of the company had posted a video of the data subject on social media from the company's surveillance system. As a result, the controller was fined a total of 49,322 RON (equivalent to €10,000).

The Belgian DPA issued a warning in response to violations of Articles 5(1)(b) and 5(1)(c) GDPR, Article 6(1) GDPR and Article 13(1)(c) GDPR committed by an employer, who had continued to use their employee’s e-mail address for company purposes following the termination of the employment contract.

The Luxembourgish DPA issued a fine of €2,500 to two public bodies due to their usage of geolocation systems to track vehicles used by their employees. The DPA found a violation of Article 5(1)(b) GDPR, Article 5(1)(c) GDPR and Article 13 GDPR.

In one of the cookie banner mass complaints filed by noyb, the Berlin DPA found that collection of consent by the controller did not fully comply with the GDPR. However, given the improvements in the cookie banner, the DPA did not adopt any corrective measure.

The Austrian DPA ordered a controller to erase the personal data of a data subject processed upon accepting a cookie via a banner in violation of the GDPR and to inform third party providers of the erasure according to Article 17 GDPR and Article 19 GDPR.

The Austrian DPA ordered a controller to bring its cookie banner into compliance with Article 7 GDPR and to inform third party providers of the deletion of personal data of the complainant pursuant to Article 19 GDPR.

The DPA ordered the controller to change its cookie banner to include an option to reject consent on the first layer. The GDPR was considered applicable even if the website did not offer good or services in the EU, as cookies monitor the behaviour of data subject in Europe.

On the basis of Article 36 GDPR, the French DPA issued an opinion finding a scientific research survey project to be implemented by a data controller legitimate as its processing of sensitive personal data was necessary for scientific research purposes in the public interest.

The DPC found that Airbnb Ireland UC lawfully retained the complainant's personal data after an erasure request, as it was necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims under Article 17(3)(e) GDPR.

The Croatian DPA announced two administrative fines, of EUR 20,000 and EUR 30,000, on two gambling and betting companies. Both were found to have used cookies on their websites without a legal basis. Both also failed to let visitors give or withdraw consent separately for each type of cookie, and failed to give adequate information about the cookie processing. The press release does not name the companies or say which fine went to which.

The Italian DPA issued a €90,000 fine against GFB One s.r.l., a sales agent for Vodafone Italia S.p.A. The company unlawfully activated two SIM cards without any authorisation from the data subject. This breached Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, Article 6 GDPR, Article 13 GDPR, and Article 157 of the Italian Privacy Code.

Several employees of a cooperative complained to the Italian DPA that it had not fully answered their access requests about the data and logic used to compute their pay, mileage reimbursements and the GPS-enabled work smartphones. The company said it had already supplied the documents and that its devices only record the meter location at the time of reading. The Garante found that the company had not given a suitable reply to the access requests, in breach of Articles 12 and 15 GDPR. It ordered the company to satisfy the access requests within 60 days and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000, and ordered the decision to be published.

A doctor employed by the South Tyrol health authority, suspended for not being vaccinated against Covid-19, asked to exercise his data protection rights (access, rectification, erasure) and received no timely reply. The reply came only after the Garante intervened, well beyond the one-month limit, which the authority blamed on an internal organisational mishap. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) GDPR and fined the authority EUR 10,000, also ordering publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were ordered because the conduct had ceased to have effects.

An employee complained that the municipality of San Severo published on its website three determinations listing about 140 employees with name, category and the individual productivity bonus each received. The municipality admitted a wrong interpretation of the rules and a website configuration error that kept the documents online; it removed them after the Garante's inquiry. The Garante found there was no suitable legal basis for disseminating the data, since transparency law requires only aggregate, not named, publication. It fined the municipality EUR 10,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.

A parent complained that the bank did not answer his access request for his minor son's personal data, which had been sent to the bank's general certified email address and was lost at a branch through an operational error. The bank only replied after the Garante intervened. The Garante found a breach of Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR, declared the processing unlawful and fined the bank EUR 42,000. No injunction was issued because the information had already been supplied, and the decision is to be published.

An employee complained that his employer used a fingerprint system to record attendance without giving information or asking consent. The Garante found that the company processed biometric data of 13 employees from February 2019 to April 2022 without a valid legal basis and with an information notice that did not mention the biometric processing. It fined the company EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision. The company had replaced the system with badges during the proceedings.

The DPA fined VODAFONE €56,000 for sharing confidential data of another customer while addressing a different customer's right of access. The controller benefitted from a €14,000 reduction in the original fine as they renounced to any form of appeal against the sanction

The Danish DPA reprimanded a regional administration for providing access to a health database to more than 16,000 staff members, in lack of a substantial connection between the tasks of the latter and the information processed.

The Spanish DPA fined BBVA €70,000 for not securely verifying the data subject's identity. A third party who had stolen the data subject's identity able to withdraw money, violating Article 6 and Article 32 GDPR.

The Spanish DPA issued a reprimand to Servicio Canario De La Salud. Medical records had been improperly accessed and the diagnosis disclosed to third parties, violating Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR.

The Slovenian DPA ordered the Agency of the Republic of Slovenia for Public Legal Records and Related Services to comply with the complainant’s deletion request under Article 17 GDPR. Contrary to national law, the Agency had published the complainant’s full address, instead of only the country of residence.

The Spanish DPA reprimanded the General Secretariat of Penitentiary Institutions of Spain for the leak of images captured by the video surveillance system of the penitentiary center of Villena (Alicante), violating Article 32 GDPR.

Following a request for prior consultation under Article 36 GDPR, the French DPA authorised the University of Bordeaux to implement automated processing of personal data for a study comparing health trajectories leading to cardio-metabolic diseases, to evaluate the interoperability of European health data.

The Cypriot DPA reprimanded the controller, Freedom Finance Europe Ltd, fro breaching Article 12(3) GDPR, since it failed to notify the data subject that her erasure request was satisfied, as well as Article 24(1) GDPR, given that the controller should have implemented appropriate measures to tackle GDPR requests.

Datatilsynet in Norway carried out an unannounced inspection of a candy store and ordered a ban on CCTV surveillance and transparent information to data subjects, as these were predominately employees younger than 18 years old.

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint regarding automatic number plate recognition cameras, because the complaint did not meet the criteria of having had a "high personal impact" on the data subject within the meaning of Article 35 GDPR.
The DPA held that video surveillance in a school during hours of operation lacked a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR and ordered a restriction on processing from all cameras during school hours.
The Oslo District Court rejected Meta’s request to issue a temporary injunction against the Norwegian DPA’S earlier ban on behavioural advertisement under Article 6(1)(b) and (f) GDPR.

A complainant objected to the University of Iceland's surveillance cameras inside and outside its buildings and to the lack of signs and information about them. After a complaint, written exchanges and an on-site inspection in April 2023, the DPA found that the university's signage and information on electronic monitoring did not meet the GDPR transparency requirements. It ordered the university to fix its signs and provide the Article 13 information, and imposed an administrative fine of ISK 1,500,000, taking into account the scale of the system (97 cameras), the number of people affected and the long duration, offset by some mitigating factors.

The processing of a minor's personal data by a bank, for the purpose of a of a 'baby loan', was lawful under Article 6(1)(c) GDPR as the bank was legally obligated to collect the minor's personal data under domestic law.
The Belgian DPA ordered a controller to comply with an access request under Article 15(1) GDPR and an erasure request under Article 17(1) GDPR, after the controller failed to facilitate the requests.

The Finnish DPA fined a psychotherapist €1,600 for not complying with a data subject's access request regarding treatment history and notes made during the sessions, within the Article 12(3) GDPR time limit. Moreover, the DPA declared that the therapist had breached Article 12(4) GDPR, as they did not inform the data subject of the reasons for non-compliance.
The Hellenic DPA reprimanded electricity supplier, "VOLTON Hellenic Energy Joint Stock Company," because they failed to adequately respond to three access requests.
The Icelandic DPA held that the Directorate of Fisheries acted in violation of Article 6(1) GDPR and Article 5(1)(a) GDPR by recording the crew of a fishing vessel during an inspection.
The Croatian DPA imposed two administrative fines in the amounts of €20,000 and €30,000 on a gambling and a betting company, due to unlawful data processing via cookies on their websites.

The Spanish DPA fined a controller for providing incomplete information about the use of video cameras. Article 13 GDPR was breached since the sign contained no information about the identity of the controller nor how to exercise data subjects' rights.

Following the an EDPB binding decision, the Irish DPA fined TikTok €345 million for several violations concerning the principles of fairness, transparency and privacy-by-default in the context of processing activities involving data of minors.
The DPA reprimanded the City of Helsinki for making user profiles publicly searchable and visible to all through the platform's own search function when this was not necessary.

A man complained that the local bar association published court hearing notices on its website naming him and his wife as defendants in criminal proceedings, and that these remained searchable on Google. The Garante found that publishing this criminal-offence data had no legal basis under Art. 10 GDPR and Art. 2-octies of the Code, and breached the principles of Art. 5(1)(a), (c) and (f). It declared the processing unlawful and fined the bar association EUR 8,000. A note at the top says the Court of Taranto later reduced the fine to EUR 8,000 (the amount in the decision itself).

A patient complained that a private medical centre (a sole proprietorship) ignored his requests for access, rectification, erasure and restriction after his Covid swab report showed a wrong birth date and tax code. The report was also first emailed to a wrong, unauthorised address. The Garante found breaches of accuracy, security, lawful basis for health data and data subject rights, and fined the former owner EUR 10,000. No corrective measures were ordered since the business had been deleted from the register and the Covid emergency had ended. The decision is published in full.

A parent complained that the online newspaper Il Giorno published a photo of girls, minors who had been harassed on a train, with only their eyes pixelated, so that they could be recognised. The Garante found that the photo was excessive and not justified by information needs, breaching the journalistic rules on minors and the fairness principle in Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. It banned further processing of the image, including in the online archive, and fined the publisher EUR 25,000. It took no action on the photo's removal, since the publisher took it down, although it was briefly republished by mistake. The Court of Cassation later rejected the publisher's challenge.

A woman complained that the Corriere della Sera website, run by RCS Mediagroup, published a photo of a deceased actress's handwritten will showing her name, date of birth and home address as a witness. The Garante found that publishing these identifying details went beyond what the news story needed and breached the principle of essentiality of information and lawfulness and fairness. It found the complaint well-founded on this point but unfounded on the failure to reply to her rights requests, which it excused as the request was unclear. It banned further processing of the complainant's name, birth date and address in the article and fined RCS Mediagroup EUR 10,000.

The Italian DPA issued a reprimand under Article 58(2)(b) GDPR to the controller, an association for medical personnel. The controller was found to have breached Article 17(1) GDPR as it continued to process the data of the complainant and renewed his membership - despite the complainant’s request to delete his personal data.
The Spanish DPA fined a resident €1,500 for installing a camera in a common area, without following the mandatory legal requirements to do so, violating Article 6(1) and Article 13 GDPR.
The Spanish DPA fined €300 for installing security cameras that focused beyond the private property of the controller's, violating Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

A complaint was lodged with the Polish DPA about a company's failure to answer a data subject's access request. In that complaint case the DPA repeatedly asked the company for explanations, and the company never supplied them, even after a phone call with its data protection officer and a promise to complete the answer. The DPA opened a separate own-initiative procedure and found that the company breached Article 31 and Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR by not cooperating and not giving access to the information needed. It fined the company PLN 56,592 (about EUR 12,000), treating the failure to give access as the most serious breach, with the company's two earlier reprimands and continued passivity as aggravating.
The Spanish DPA fined an individual €10,000 for publishing a video of a data subject in a vulnerable situation, without his consent, violating Article 6 (1) GDPR.

IMY received a tip that customer documents of the insurer Moderna Försäkringar (now Trygg-Hansa) could be accessed by unauthorised people. Between October 2018 and February 2021 the insurer's technical measures were inadequate, so data on about 650,000 customers, including health data and personal identity numbers, was exposed. IMY found breaches of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of SEK 35 million, set well below the cap based on the Tryg group's turnover because the breach concerned only a limited part of the business.

The Swedish DPA issued a penalty fee of SEK 35 million (around €3 million) against Trygg-Hansa. The insurance company had serious security flaws via faulty URLs resulting in a data breach of 650,000 customers' data over a period of two years.

The Spanish DPA fined a Community €1,500 for unduly exposure of personal data to third parties that appeared in a judgement that was placed on a public bulletin board, in violation of Article 5(1)(f) and Article 32 GDPR.
During an own volition inquiry into processing activities carried out by the Galway County Council, the DPC found violations of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR, Article 24 GDPR and Article 35(1) GDPR.

The Romanian authority investigated UiPath SRL after it notified a personal data breach: the data of about 600,000 users of its Academy platform was exposed on a third-party website for about 10 days because storage settings allowed unauthorised access. The authority found breaches of Articles 25 and 32 GDPR, acting as lead authority under Article 60. It fined the company RON 346,598 (EUR 70,000) and ordered it to set up a regular process for testing and evaluating the effectiveness of its security measures.

The Spanish DPA ordered a controller to reply to a data subject's request to delete personal data, to an objection of processing of data for marketing purposes, transfer to third parties and profiling

The Belgian DPA dismissed a complaint, despite the existence of GDPR violations. The DPA was of the opinion that the breaches did not result in a "major social and/or personal impact," thus the resources required to investigate the complaint would be disproportionate.

The Information Commissioner’s Office (ICO) reprimanded Nottinghamshire County Council for infringing Article 32(1) (UK) GDPR. The failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures resulted in a social worker sharing unredacted copies of their assessment report to a mother and her two ex-partners, each the father of one of the two children mentioned in the report.

The DPA found a school to have breached the principle of data minimisation for processing the bank account numbers of all its students for the purpose of awarding possible scholarships concerning only some of them.

The Croatian DPA held that a media outlet unlawfully processed personal data of a data subject as the data was not publicly available and the public interest did not prevail over the right to privacy of the data subject.
The Belgian DPA found a violation of Article 21(2) GDPR when a controller did not respect the data subject's right to object to direct marketing.

The Belgian DPA found violations of Articles 5(2), 13(1)(a), 37(1)(a), 37(7), and 39 GDPR by a municipal school because it had failed to assign a data protection officer and correctly document compliance with the GDPR.

The DPA held that the complete surveillance of a residential complex to prevent theft and keep strangers out of the building is a serious interference with the fundamental right to privacy of the data subjects.
The DPA held that the operator of a job application platform and recruiters making use of such a platform are not joint controllers for the processing of job applicants

The DPA reprimanded the City of Helsinki for failing to conclude a data processing agreement with the company that maintained the city's online pupil welfare service, which allowed pupils to contact a school counsellor or school psychologist.

The Belgian DPA determined that two public controllers violated several GDPR provisions for sharing personal data in order to issue a parking fine. Both controllers did not have a legal basis for such processing and did not provide adequate transparency to the data subject.

The Belgian DPA issued a warning to a hospital group for non-compliance of Article 32 GDPR and Article 24 GDPR, as the hospital group had failed to implement the appropriate internal data security measures.

The Norwegian DPA held that transfers of personal data to the United States in the context of Google Analytics were illegal, as the controller failed to implement sufficient protective measures in addition to SCCs.
The Maltese DPA held that the use of personal data for a legal claim is incompatible with the household exemption under Article 2(2)(c) GDPR.
The Luxembourg DPA found the Municipal Administration of Leudelange to have breached Articles 37(1)(a) and 37(7) GDPR, since the latter, on the date of investigation, had not yet designated a DPO.

The HDPA ordered a city council in Greece to cease their processing activities, under Article 58(2) GDPR and Article 15(8) of Law 4624/2019, because of an unresolved data breach, which allowed unauthorised users to access citizens' personal data via URL manipulation.

The Maltese DPA decided that a controller, sending personal schoolwork to a data subject's personal email adress with other people in the "cc", is an infringement of Article 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(b) GDPR.

The CNIL approved a reference methodology for health data processing by organisations acting within a framework of legitimate interests. This methodology will ensure that the privacy of individuals is protected while simultaneously facilitating researchers when accessing the National Health Data System.

The CNIL has adopted two new reference methodologies to enable public bodies (MR-007) to process data from the main database of the National Health Data System(SNDS), beyond the Medicalization of Information Systems Program (PMSI). The MR-007 reference methodology governs access by organizations acting within the framework of their public interest mission to data from the main database of the National Health Data System.
The Irish DPC found that Airbnb was in violation of Articles 5, 12, 15 and 17 GDPR for an incomplete response to an access request and delays in addressing an erasure request. No fine was issued.

Following a request for erasure, the controller failed to take reasonable steps to inform online media outlets to erase the applicant's personal data. The Slovenian DPA found a violation of the right to be forgotten under Article 17(2) GDPR.
The Spanish DPA fined HOLALUZ €70,000 for unlawful data processing without consent by registering the electricity supplies of several properties of the data subject, violating Article 6(1) GDPR.

A citizen complained about the video surveillance system near waste containers in the municipality of Modica. The municipality had hired Cat s.r.l. to supply, manage and maintain the cameras and to analyse the footage. The company acted on the municipality's behalf without a valid Article 28 agreement defining its role as processor, since its appointment as judicial police auxiliary did not meet Article 28 requirements. The Garante found processing without a lawful basis and in breach of the lawfulness principle, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

A resident of Modica reported video devices placed near waste bins. The Municipality had hired a sole-trader firm to supply, run and maintain the cameras and analyse the footage. The firm processed personal data for the Municipality for about six months from March 2020 without an Article 28 processor agreement; appointment as judicial police auxiliary did not meet Article 28 requirements. The Garante found processing without a lawful basis and in breach of the lawfulness principle, and fined the firm EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision.

A health trust in the Milan area notified the Garante of three data breaches: a disability-assessment summons sent to the wrong person, a Multiple Sclerosis Centre email sent to 198 patients with addresses visible in the cc field, and a lab result handed to the wrong patient, which led to a false pre-diabetes diagnosis. The Garante joined the three proceedings and rejected the trust's defence arguments. It found unlawful communication of health data in breach of Articles 5(1)(f), 9 and 32 GDPR. It imposed a single fine of EUR 12,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No corrective orders were imposed because the conduct had ended and the trust had adopted further measures.
The Italian DPA fined €40,000 Compara Facile s.r.l. for having performed marketing phone calls in without collecting informed consent from the data subjects.

The Italian DPA fined an Italian telecommunications company €100,000 following a control of marketing and profiling activities. According to the DPA, the company was unlawfully processing consumers´ data.

A resident complained that the municipality of Modica sent him fines for wrongly depositing waste, based on video recorded by cameras near waste bins, with the footage reviewed over a month later and with inadequate information signs. The Garante found that the municipality used the cameras in a non-compliant way from August 2017 to May 2021: inadequate privacy notices, excessive retention, no proper processor agreements with the camera contractors, and late appointment and publication of the data protection officer. It fined the municipality EUR 45,000 and ordered publication of the decision on the Garante's website.
The Italian DPA authorised a hospital to conduct medical research relating to personal data of contactable and uncontactable (deceased) data subjects.

A woman complained that she kept receiving promotional calls on behalf of Maximum International Corp. S.r.l. without consent, even after objecting, and that her access and erasure requests went unanswered. The company denied being the controller, saying independent agencies sell its products. The Garante held Maximum to be the controller and found failures of accountability, of data subject rights handling, of consent for the calls, and of consent on its website form, where marketing and profiling consent was mandatory. It banned processing of website data without valid consent, ordered erasure and corrective measures, and fined the company EUR 5,000, with publication of the decision.
The Spanish DPA fined a company €10,000 for recording and publishing images of minors on its social media without having the consent of their parents.
The Belgian DPA considered that collecting names and dates of birth of tourists was not necessary to establish the amount of a tax calculated on the basis of the number of occupants.

The EDPS found, after the CJEU requested for an authorisation of contractual clauses under Article 48(3)(a) of the EU GDPR, that no data transfers took place that would fall under the scope of such authorisation in the context of the CJEU’s use of the videoconferencing tool Cisco Webex.

The Athens Medical Association (AMA) collected its members' Covid-19 vaccination certificates to comply with domestic public health legislation. The Hellenic DPA (HDPA) held that the processing carried out by was lawful for the purposes of Article 6(1)(e) GDPR.
The Spanish DPA fined a security guard €10,000 for capturing images from the video surveillance system of a correctional facility and disseminating them via WhatsApp, in violation of Article 6 GDPR.

The Polish DPA imposed a fine of €2,640 against a controller for not notifying data subjects of a breach and for not informing the DPA within the 72 hour time-limit, in violation of Articles 33 and 34 GDPR. Furthermore, the controller breached the principle of accountability, as they were unable to demonstrate compliance.

The Icelandic DPA held that a bank requiring uniquely identifying information (i.e. a social security number) to avoid anonymous transactions did not violate the GDPR as the bank had a statutory obligation to do so.

The Finnish DPA ordered a telecommunications company to allow the data subjects to easily deny the use of their contact information for direct marketing purposes in connection with electronic direct marketing messages.

The Belgian DPA held that vaccination status constitutes sensitive health data under Article 9(1) GDPR and that a person who refused to provide such data has sufficient interest to submit a complaint even though no processing took place.

The Guardia di finanza inspected a restaurant company in Genga and found seven working CCTV cameras with no information signs, cameras able to film the public road, and no labour inspectorate authorisation for monitoring employees. The Garante found the processing unlawful under Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 GDPR and Article 114 of the Italian Code. No corrective orders were issued because the company had put up signs, redirected the cameras and obtained the authorisation after the inspection. It imposed a fine of EUR 5,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

An employee complained that his employer, a utility company, did not properly answer his access request for the data it used to bring a disciplinary charge against him. The charge was based on a private investigator's report, which he only learned of during his dismissal court case. The company first treated the request as one for access to the work computer, then called it generic and refused it. The Garante found breaches of fairness (Art. 5(1)(a)), Art. 12 and Art. 15, rejected the 'minor infringement' argument, and fined the company EUR 10,000, with publication of the decision.

Data collected for a risk assessment for vaccination against Monkeypox was considered a violation of the principles of lawfulness, fairness and transparency and of integrity and confidentiality (Article 5(1)(a), Article 5(1)(f) and Article 13 GDPR).

The Icelandic DPA fined the Office of the National Medical Examiner ISK 12,000,000 (approx. € 82,000) for multiple GDPR violations after a security breach on its website Heilsuvera – an online healthcare system and prescription portal.

IMY investigated a complaint, passed on from the Austrian authority, about CDON AB's website using Google Analytics. Through the tool, visitors' personal data was transferred to the USA. IMY found that the data was personal data, that CDON was the controller, and that the standard contractual clauses and CDON's supplementary measures (such as IP truncation) did not ensure the protection level required by Chapter V. It found a breach of Article 44 GDPR. It fined CDON SEK 300,000 and ordered it to bring its use of Google Analytics into line with Chapter V, in particular by stopping use of the version in use on 14 August 2020 unless sufficient safeguards are put in place.

The Swedish DPA held that by using Google Analytics provided by Google LLC, Coop breached Article 44 GDPR. SCCs and safeguards that were in place could not support data transfers to the US in a way that would not undermine the level of protection of personal data guaranteed by the GDPR.

The Swedish DPA held that by using Google Analytics provided by Google LLC, Dagens Industri breached Article 44 GDPR. SCCs and safeguards that were in place could not support data transfers to the US in a way that would not undermine the level of protection of personal data guaranteed by the GDPR.

The Swedish DPA held that by using Google Analytics provided by Google LLC, Tele2 Sverige breached Article 44 GDPR. SCCs and safeguards that were in place could not support data transfers to the US in a way that would not undermine the level of protection of personal data guaranteed by the GDPR.

A gynaecologist replied publicly to a patient's critical online review and revealed her diagnosis. The reply stayed visible at least until 3 October 2022. The Austrian DPA found that this was unlawful processing of health data and breached the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation and data minimisation. It held the act was intentional. It imposed a fine of EUR 10,000 (336 hours substitute imprisonment) plus EUR 1,000 procedural costs, using an estimated income because he did not disclose his finances.

The DPA held that Google must delete nine specified links from its search results under Article 17 GDPR, as the data subject's “particular situation” outweighed public interest. Furthermore, the DPA confirmed its jurisdiction despite Google having no EU establishment.

The DPA ordered Google to delete links appearing in search results for the data subject's name. Additionally, the DPA ordered Google to amend it's deletion request process by enabling the submission of attachments, providing direct contact information and ceasing automated responses.

The DPA reprimanded a controller for not providing access to all data processed about the data subject. The controller explained how to request the missing data, but the DPA considered this procedure overly complicated.
The Spanish DPA fined a controller €2,000 for infringing Article 13 GDPR in their contract with a tenant.

Persónuvernd published a summary of its decision of 2 May 2023 closing a security audit of the Icelandic Health Insurance agency. The agency had fixed the issues it was ordered to correct. Two serious weaknesses existing at the time of the on-site inspection, lack of multi-factor authentication for staff and healthcare providers accessing health data systems and use of real data in development and test environments, were found to breach Articles 5(1)(f), 32 and 25 GDPR. An administrative fine of ISK 2 million was imposed. The fine decision and the audit decision themselves are not published for information security reasons.

According to the Belgian DPA, a US-based controller whose activity includes the organisation of conferences in Europe is subject to the GDPR and must, among other obligations, appoint a representative.

A debt collection company sent default information on small consumer loans issued by a Danish lender to the credit bureau Creditinfo Lánstraust. The loan terms lacked the required clause permitting default registration, and some claims were below the minimum amount allowed for registration. About 2,000 people were affected. Persónuvernd found the processing had no legal basis and breached the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle, and fined the company ISK 3,500,000. The company did not respond to the authority's letters.

Persónuvernd examined how eCommerce 2020 ApS, a Danish small-loan company, sent loan defaults to the Icelandic credit bureau Creditinfo Lánstraust. Between July 2018 and May 2019 its loan terms lacked the required clause allowing default registration, and claims below the minimum amount (577 individuals) were also reported. The authority held that the company was the controller and had no valid legal basis, and breached the lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle. It imposed an administrative fine of ISK 7,500,000, taking into account the number of data subjects (about 2,000), the burdensome nature of the processing and the company's reduced activity.

The Icelandic DPA ruled on a complaint by the Consumers' Association about the credit bureau Creditinfo Lánstraust hf. registering defaults on small loans granted by eCommerce 2020 ApS. The bureau recorded the claims although the loan terms lacked the clause required by its operating licence for registering defaults, and some claims were below the minimum amount. It had not adequately checked that the registration conditions were met and deleted the entries late. The DPA found a breach of lawfulness and accountability and fined the company ISK 37,856,900, 2.5% of its 2021 turnover.
The DPA fined a media company SEK 13,000,000 for unlawfully profiling its users in order to target them with behavioral advertising on its website, thus violating Article 6(1) GDPR.
The DPA reprimanded a controller for not appropriately clarifying whether its processing operations were based on consent or a contract.

Due to an error within a digital identity solution used nationwide, several citizens accidentally gained access to bank accounts of another person. The Danish DPA held that only recommending and not requiring a mandatory validation of tokens for the safe use, which would eliminate the error, the solution violated Article 32 GDPR.

The Belgian DPA confirmed that CCTV images made to protect against littering and illegal dumping can be used to fine a data subject doing the littering, based on public interest under Article 6(1)(e) GDPR. The DPA also noted that person combining the roles of DPO and safety consultant could pose a breach of Article 38(6) GDPR.

The Italian DPA imposed a fine of €1,000,000 on Autostrade per l'Italia for erroneously indicating the developer of a toll reimbursement app as the controller. The DPA also found a violation of the principles of lawfulness and transparency.

Digi reported a data breach in September 2019: an attacker exploited a years-old known vulnerability in its content management system on digi.hu and reached databases of about 322,000 people, mostly a test database that should have been deleted after use. The authority had fined Digi HUF 100 million in 2020; after the CJEU (C-77/21) and the Budapest Tribunal found no purpose-limitation violation, the authority repeated the procedure on the sanctions. It found violations of storage limitation (Art. 5(1)(e)) and security of processing (Art. 32(1)-(2)), ordered Digi to review all its databases for the need for encryption, and fined it HUF 80 million (4/5 of the original). The decision is to be published with the controller's identity.
The Hungarian DPA reduced a fine issued in response to data breach from 100,000,000 HUF to 80,000,000 HUF (equivalent to €200,000) following a re-evaluation after CJEU decision Case C-77/21.

On the basis of the Austrian data protection law implementing Article 89 GDPR, the Austrian DPA held that processing activities supporting scientific research in the field of automated driving shall be authorised by the supervisory authority itself.

The Polish DPA was handling a complaint about a company passing a person's data to a third party without a legal basis. It twice asked the company for explanations, but the company never collected the registered letters, so they were deemed delivered, and it never answered. The DPA opened separate proceedings and found that the company breached Article 58(1)(a) and (e) GDPR by not giving the authority access to the information it needed. It imposed an administrative fine of PLN 33,012 (about EUR 7,000), citing the continuing, negligent failure and complete lack of cooperation.

The DPA reprimanded an employer for the usage of vague language in its privacy policy creating the false impression that the processing of employment data is based on consent rather than the performance of the employment contract.
The Spanish DPA fined a logistics company €50,000 for installing videocameras in the employees' rest area, in violation of Article 6 GDPR.

Romania's ANSPDCP, acting as lead authority after the Hungarian DPA referred three complaints against Dante International SA (the emag online shop), found that the company failed to facilitate and honour erasure requests, gave incomplete information on third-country transfers, and kept using a complainant's email address without consent. It fined the company RON 148,830 (EUR 30,000) for Articles 12(2) and 17(1) and RON 49,610 (EUR 10,000) for Article 6(1)(a), and issued a warning for Articles 13 and 14. It also ordered corrective measures: complete privacy information, an anonymisation method, and regular staff training across the group.
The Belgian DPA decided that subjective statements made in a meeting and faithfully recorded in the minutes do not fall within the scope of Article 16 GDPR.

A pharmacist complained to the Belgian DPA that the Order of Pharmacists kept data about a disciplinary sanction imposed on him and refused his erasure request. The Litigation Chamber found that the processing infringed the principles of Article 5(1)(a) to (e) GDPR, among other things because the Order never checked whether the sanction, based on the old code of ethics, was still accurate and relevant after the new code was adopted. It fined the Order EUR 30,000 (reduced from the EUR 50,000 first proposed), ordered erasure of the sanction data from the complainant's disciplinary file and ordered the Order to bring its processing into line with Article 5(1). The decision is published with the Order identified.
